News decomposition of a nowcast revision between two data vintages

Source: R/news.R
mfbdfm_news.Rd

Answers the question every high-frequency indicator raises: the nowcast moved this week – which release did that? Between the data vintage a fit was estimated on and a newer one, reports for every newly released observation its actual value, the forecast the old vintage implied for it, the news (actual minus forecast), the gain that news carries on the target, and the resulting impact on the nowcast. The impacts add up to the revision.

Usage

mfbdfm_news(
  fit,
  new_data,
  stocks = NULL,
  period = NULL,
  by = c("series", "group"),
  groups = NULL,
  new_fit = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'mfbdfm_news'
print(x, n_show = 10, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mfbdfm_news'
as.data.frame(
  x,
  row.names = NULL,
  optional = FALSE,
  what = c("observation", "component"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mfbdfm_news'
plot(x, n_show = 10, ...)

Arguments

fit

A fitted model from ind_dfm(), estimated on the old vintage.

new_data

The new data vintage: either an mfbdfm_data() object or a named list of ts objects, carrying exactly the series fit was estimated on, at the same frequencies. Pass stocks alongside to supply the flow/stock pair instead.

stocks

Named list of ts objects treated as stock variables, or NULL. Ignored when new_data is an mfbdfm_data() object. The flow/stock split is taken from the fit's inventory in any case; this argument exists so the same call shape as ind_dfm() works.

period

Numeric (decimal time) or NULL. The target period whose nowcast revision is decomposed. Defaults to the last target period the old vintage had not yet observed.

by

Either "series" (default, one component per input series) or "group" (one component per group of series). Governs the aggregation in $by_component, print() and plot(); the per-observation detail is retained whichever is chosen.

groups

Optional named character vector or list mapping every series name to a group name, used when by = "group" and the inventory has no group or category column.

new_fit

Optional fit from ind_dfm() on the new vintage. Supply it to get the parameter term; without it that term is NA.

x

An object of class "mfbdfm_news".

n_show

Number of components to list, ordered by absolute impact.

...

Passed on to the underlying plotting calls; ignored by print() and as.data.frame().

row.names, optional

Ignored, present for consistency with the generic.

what

Either "observation" (default) for the per-observation tidy table with its summary rows, or "component" for the impacts aggregated to by.

Value

An object of class "mfbdfm_news", a list with

table

The tidy table as.data.frame() returns: one row per newly released or revised observation with term, series, group, time, actual, forecast, news, gain and impact, followed by summary rows for the total revision and the parameter term.

news, revisions

The two per-observation blocks on their own.

by_component

Impacts aggregated to by: the component column, news, revision and their sum impact.

totals

One row: nowcast_old, revision, news, total, parameter, nowcast_new, posterior_old, posterior_new.

period, target, by, components, n_added, n_revised, model, call

Metadata.

With print(), as.data.frame() and plot() (a waterfall) methods.

Details

Conditional on the parameters, the factor path and the unobserved data entries are jointly Gaussian with a sparse precision Q (the samplers' own matrices; see mfbdfm_contributions(), which uses the same construction). Writing z = (f, x) and splitting it into the entries an observation pins and the latent rest,

$$E[z_L \mid y] = -Q_{LL}^{-1} Q_{LO}\, y, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(z_L \mid y) = Q_{LL}^{-1}.$$

A new vintage observes some of those latent entries. Conditioning the same Gaussian on them gives, for the target entry k and the newly released set N,

$$\mathrm{gain} = \Sigma_{kN}\,\Sigma_{NN}^{-1}, \qquad \mathrm{impact} = \mathrm{gain} \times (\mathrm{actual} - \mathrm{forecast}),$$

with Sigma = Q_LL^-1. This is Bańbura and Modugno's (2014) decomposition with the Kalman smoother replaced by the stacked form this package samples in. The orthogonalisation through Sigma_NN^-1 is what makes the impacts add up: several series are released in the same week and their forecast errors are correlated, so a per-observation weight that ignored that would not sum to the revision.

Nothing is refitted and Q is never inverted. One sparse Cholesky factorisation of Q_LL serves every quantity above, with one solve per newly released observation – a handful for a weekly vintage update. The cost is linear in how much the new vintage adds, so this is a tool for consecutive vintages; handing it a vintage that adds a year of data asks for a year's worth of solves.

Two things are deliberately not carried over from the sampler. The factor draw masks the forecast horizon with a selection vector, because it conditions on the sampler's own augmented data and has to stop the extension periods' imputed values from feeding back into the factor. Here only genuine observations are conditioned on and everything else is left latent, which is the correct marginal and needs no mask. And the sampler pins observed entries with a 1e-9 observation variance; this conditions on them exactly, which is the limit that nugget approximates (the two agree to O(1e-9), asserted in tests/testthat/test-news.R).

What is held fixed, and where the rest of the revision goes

The decomposition is exact at fixed parameters, which is standard practice and is also what makes it exact. Three things are therefore held at the old vintage's values:

  • the posterior mean parameters theta from fit;

  • the volatility path h, extended over any periods the new vintage adds by holding its last value – the posterior mean extension of a random walk;

  • the standardisation. prepare_data() standardises each series with moments computed from the vintage in hand, so the new vintage is re-prepared with the fit's inventory. Using the new vintage's own moments would make the nowcast a nonlinear function of the data and nothing would add up. The consequence is that the change in standardisation is part of the parameter term below, not of any series' impact. This looks like a bug later if it is not written down, so it is written down here.

What is left over is reported rather than folded in:

news

Per newly released observation, as above. Exact by construction.

revision

Per observation present in both vintages whose value changed. Also exact and also additive per observation: at a fixed observation set the plug-in nowcast is linear in the data, so a revised value contributes its own weight times its own change. (The plan for this feature expected only a block total here; it is finer than that.)

parameter

nowcast(theta_new) - nowcast(theta_old), the part of the revision that comes from re-estimating the model rather than from new data. It needs a fit on the new vintage, so it is NA unless new_fit is supplied.

The nowcast reported here is the plug-in one

nowcast_old and nowcast_new are E[x_target | y, theta-hat], the nowcast with the posterior mean parameters plugged in. fit$nowcast is the mean of the nowcast over the posterior of theta, which is a different number; it is carried alongside as posterior_old so the two can be compared rather than confused. The decomposition adds up to the plug-in revision, which is the only revision it can add up to.

Which period

One target period at a time: the gain is a row of the smoother's weight matrix and that row belongs to one period. period defaults to the last target period the old vintage had not yet observed – the nowcast, in other words. Pass a decimal time to pick another. A period whose target value the old vintage already observed is an error: its nowcast is pinned to the observation and no amount of news can move it.

fcast_dfm() is deferred

Deliberately, and not for want of algebra – the same derivation applies. The target is not identified in that model: fcast_dfm()'s target argument only selects which series' nowcast is surfaced, and the factors are pinned by a post-hoc Procrustes plus varimax rotation rather than during sampling. A gain computed at a fixed theta would be a gain in a rotation the new vintage's fit does not reproduce, so "the impact of this release on the factor" needs a rule for aligning rotations across vintages first. That is a second methodological question, tracked separately; an fcast_dfm fit is an informative error here rather than a plausible-looking number.

References

Bańbura, M., & Modugno, M. (2014). Maximum likelihood estimation of factor models on datasets with arbitrary pattern of missing data. Journal of Applied Econometrics, 29(1), 133-160. doi:10.1002/jae.2306

Kronenberg, P. (2026). A weekly activity index for Switzerland. Swiss Journal of Economics and Statistics, 162:10. doi:10.1186/s41937-026-00157-w

See also

mfbdfm_contributions() for the decomposition of the level of the factor and nowcast (the same weight matrix, applied to the data rather than to the news), cut_data_real_time() to build vintage pairs, and ind_dfm().

Other model functions: mfbdfm_contributions(), mfbdfm_diagnostics(), mfbdfm_draws

Examples

# \donttest{
data(mfbdfm_example_data)

# two consecutive vintages of the shipped example data: the old one stops
# four weeks earlier, so the new one brings four weeks of releases
new <- mfbdfm_example_data
old <- new
old$flows <- lapply(old$flows, function(x)
  if(stats::frequency(x) > 4) stats::window(x, end = stats::time(x)[length(x) - 4])
  else x)
old$stocks <- lapply(old$stocks, function(x)
  stats::window(x, end = stats::time(x)[length(x) - 4]))

set.seed(1)
fit <- ind_dfm(old, length_sample = 50, burn_in = 10)
